work.text: In 1832, the French Romantic artist Eugène Delacroix was invited to accompany the Count de Mornay, ambassador to the Sultan of Morocco, on a journey to Spain, Morocco, and Algeria. … The drawing was one of 18 that Delacroix included in an album given to the count as a souvenir of their travels.

source.author: The Cleveland Museum of Art
source.title: A Young Black Woman Fetching Water

work.text: During the three months that the expedition lasted he filled his note-books with drawings and notes of architecture, costumes, faces, and effects of light, shade and colour.

moment.text: He went not primarily to study art, but to escape from the civilization of Paris, in hopes of seeing a more "primitive" culture. He eventually produced over 100 paintings and drawings of scenes from or based on the life of the people of North Africa, and added a new and personal chapter to the interest in Orientalism.

The memories and documents he brought back from this journey enabled him henceforth to depict … oriental scenes with an accent of truth hitherto unknown, for, as Gautier says, Delacroix was the discoverer of Africa, from a picturesque point of view.

matters.text: The aspect of this country will remain for ever in my eyes … all my life long the men of this noble race will live and move in my memory

source.author: Eugène Delacroix

matters.text: The Greeks and Romans are here at my door, in the Arabs who wrap themselves in a white blanket and look like Cato or Brutus
While there, he created this watercolor depicting a young woman—likely an enslaved African—as she engaged in domestic work.
